entries.title: FIFA president Gianni Infantino drops plans to sell World Cup profits to private equity
entries.summary: <p>ZURICH — FIFA President Gianni Infantino is abandoning his divisive plan to sell World Cup profits to private equity after receiving pushback from all corners of the soccer world.</p><p>Infantino's decision came after his senior adviser who sat on a White House panel resigned and Asia's soccer body joined Europe and North America in opposing it.</p><p>"Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place," Infantino said in a statement on Friday. "Our purpose has always been — and will always be — to unite and improve. As a result, this proposal will not proceed."</p><p>Infantino had proposed creating a $20 billion company to run the World Cup with private investors including the Kushner family, but drew backlash that grew every day since Tuesday's announcement.</p><p>UEFA's 55 member nations agreed to boycott the World Cup and all other FIFA competitions over Infantino's plan on Thursday. North America's CONCACAF and the Asian Football Confederation also said they opposed the plan.</p><p>"Some things are simply too important to sell," UEFA said in a statement. "The FIFA World Cup belongs to football. It always will. And so long as Europe has a voice, it will never be for sale."</p><p>Infantino's senior adviser, Carlos Cordeiro, a former Goldman Sachs banker who represented the soccer body on the White House Task Force for the World Cup, resigned on Friday and urged other senior FIFA staff to speak out.</p><p>"I cannot stand by while FIFA considers selling a stake in the World Cup," Cordeiro said in a statement, just hours after FIFA insisted: "Nobody is selling football."<br></p>

entries.title: Welch’s pledge to help CTU sets off alarm bells
entries.summary: <p>House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch promised the Chicago Teachers Union last week that he will “lead” the effort to send more <a class="Link" href="https://news.wttw.com/2026/07/31/illinois-house-speaker-welch-committed-more-funding-cps-school-board-banking-it" target="_blank" >state money to Chicago Public Schools</a> during the upcoming fall veto session.</p><p>Welch made his pledge in a CTU-posted video Wednesday while holding a union poster blasting proposed CPS layoffs and budget cuts. “The state of Illinois underfunds Chicago schools by $2 billion,” the poster proclaimed.</p><p>“This should not be happening,” Welch said, gesturing toward the sign focusing on layoffs. “I do think that the state of Illinois can do better, should do better. This should be, and I’m going to keep fighting for you, so that we can get more revenue to get to CPS schools … I will lead that effort in the veto session.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c20000" name="module-c20000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>Welch, of course, has been <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/07/28/illinois-house-speaker-emanuel-chris-welch-harry-benton-michael-j-madigan-sexual-harassment-inquiry" >under fire for weeks</a> because, among other things, he waited almost three years after then-Rep. Harry Benton, D-Plainfield, was accused of sexual harassment to take any sort of action. He’s also faced heat for inappropriate personal interactions with the alleged victim. He obviously needs allies.</p><p>But any tax hike and/or supplemental appropriations bills with immediate effective dates would require three-fifths votes in both chambers during veto session — making Welch’s pledge ring more than a little hollow and setting off alarm bells among some of his members.</p><p>“Getting flashbacks of the Madigan experience where the speaker stops saying no to everyone to desperately keep his job,” one suburban House member who asked for anonymity told me.</p><p>Indeed, when Michael Madigan was under fire, he regularly agreed to put his weight behind legislation favored by groups of members, which directly led to things like hundreds of millions of dollars in state-paid healthcare for undocumented immigrants.</p><p>“I think his idea is laughable,” said one exurban House Democrat when contacted by my associate Isabel Miller.</p><p>“How is a vote that excludes every suburban district that is having to make hard choices good for the caucus?” a suburban Democrat asked.</p><p>Not all suburbanites were so negative. Progressive Rep. Dagmara Avelar, D-Bolingbrook, told Isabel, “I am in support of making sure all our schools in need are funded, and I’m looking forward to actively discuss the resources needed to tackle this issue during veto.”</p><p>Welch’s people and some of his allies have been privately putting pressure on skeptical members to stay quiet during this Benton-related uproar, and according to sources, give Welch time to “let this all blow over.”</p><p>Welch did not consult with his caucus before making his CTU pledge, and some see it as temporarily benefiting himself while setting up his members to look bad this fall when his unilateral promise can’t be kept. Never show weakness.</p><p>And how hard can Welch push members to help him fulfill this new pledge while also pressuring members to stay in line on the questions that continue to swirl around him?</p><p>The day after Welch made that commitment to the CTU, the CPS Board voted to pass a budget that relies on the state increasing funding by $150 million in the next few months. The CTU supported the vote.</p><p>But as I told you above, Welch did not seek buy-in from his caucus before making the pledge, and finding a three-fifths super-majority to spend even $150 million that the state doesn’t currently have to bail out Chicago doesn’t seem possible. Besides the obvious regional rivalries, and the fact that CPS put itself into this position by using temporary pandemic money for its permanent base spending, lots of legislators were disappointed in May with the appropriated funding for their cherished programs.</p><p>So, if the CTU wants to increase revenue, then it’s gonna be a whole lot more than $150 million. And then they’d have to find 71 votes in the House and 36 in the Senate to pay for it.</p><p>The CTU is now proclaiming that they have triangulated Gov. JB Pritzker because they have both Welch and Illinois Senate President Don Harmon, D-Oak Park, on their side. But Harmon did not go nearly as far as Welch, merely committing to working with them on finding revenue.</p><p>Nevertheless, the union sent an email to members after the vote claiming that Pritzker “has been in office for eight years and owes the state's students $6.4 billion dollars from pre-K to Ph.D.”</p><p>In his attempt to secure the support of a powerful ally while he’s under fire over the Benton debacle, Welch may have inadvertently tossed the governor under the bus.</p><p>The next day, Pritzker turned the tables by saying he was waiting to see Welch’s plan.</p><p><i>Rich Miller also publishes Capitol Fax, a daily political newsletter, and CapitolFax.com.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-8c0000" name="module-8c0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. including Olivia Rodrigo on “Thirty-Three,” Yungblud on “Luna” and one-time Pumpkins bassist Melissa Auf der Maur for “The Everlasting Gaze.” </p><p>Check back tomorrow for the full review.</p><div entries.title: White Sox pound Rays for four home runs, take three-game lead in AL Central
entries.summary: <p>ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — The White Sox slugged their way to the team’s largest division lead since the end of the 2021 season, beating the American League-leading Rays 6-1 behind home runs from their Nos. 2-5 hitters in the lineup.</p><p>Miguel Vargas crushed a 433-foot solo homer to left field with two outs in the first inning. Andrew Benintendi led off the second with a solo shot. Munetaka Murakami hit a two-run shot in the third, and Colson Montgomery sent a ball 425 feet, off the catwalk above right field, for a two-run shot in the sixth.</p><p>“I wish it didn’t [hit the catwalk] because I wanted to see how far it was actually gonna go,” Montgomery said.</p><p>According to Elias, Montgomery, Murakami and Vargas homered in the same game for the fifth time this year, tying the MLB (10th time) and franchise records (second time). Joe Crede, Paul Konerko and Jose Valentin were the first Sox trio to accomplish the feat, in 2004. The Dodgers’ Cody Bellinger, Corey Seager and Joc Pederson were the last MLB trio to do so, in 2019.</p><p>“That’s real special to have those guys right in the middle of your lineup do that,” manager Will Venable said. “To be able to [hit] a really good pitcher. Take Colson, for example, first couple at-bats, [Nick Martinez] didn’t give him anything to hit at all. And then finally he got something to hit, and it was nice to see him do that.”</p><p>It also was nice for Venable to see his taxed bullpen get a break. Erick Fedde threw five innings of one-run ball, Tyler Schweitzer covered three and Trevor Richards finished it off. Sox relievers had thrown 11 innings in the previous two games combined.</p><p>Combined with the Guardians’ loss, the Sox (58-51) moved three games ahead in the Central and a season-high-tying seven games over .500.</p><h3>State of the Sox</h3><p>Venable held his monthly “State of the Sox” meeting with players this week, in which the team discussed, among other things, the trade deadline, which is at 5 p.m. Monday.</p><p>“We had some positive feedback, and really just wanted to be proactive,” Venable said before the Sox’ 6-1 victory Friday against the American League-leading Rays. “We have guys who are going through some of these things that happen during the season for the first time, and they can be a distraction.</p><p>“And there’s a non-zero chance that the DNA of our club changes over the next couple of days. We just want to be prepared for that and make sure that it’s not more of a distraction than it needs to be and that we’re focused on the things that we can control and continue to keep ourselves in a good spot down the stretch.”</p><p>All was quiet on the Sox’ trade front — whether that’s good or bad is debatable — and players said they are indeed focused on the games at hand. They need to be as they navigate a challenging stretch of 13 games against teams currently holding an AL playoff spot.</p><p>In fact, the postseason was another topic of discussion in the meeting. The players know that the Central Division is there for the taking — the Sox entered Friday with a two-game lead over the Guardians — but perhaps the AL will be there for the taking, as well.</p><p>“We’re not going to sell ourselves short,” center fielder Tristan Peters told the Sun-Times. “The goal’s the World Series, at least I think it is in every player’s mind here. I don’t know how it is in the front office or with the coaching staff. I know in my mind, our goal is to win the World Series.”</p><p>But first things first. The Sox have a trade deadline to endure.</p><p>“The first step in the path is really embracing whatever happens at the deadline as a positive thing and getting back to business and moving forward,” Venable said. “[The meeting] wasn’t a motivational message that creates belief that down the road we can be in a good spot. It was a message that, if you want to be in a good spot, the way we respond to this deadline matters.”</p><h3>Notes</h3><p>White Sox Charities will hold an online auction Tuesday to help fund recovery efforts in Kumamoto, Japan, Murakami’s hometown, which was struck by a 7.1-magnitude earthquake this week. Fans will be able to bid at whitesox.com/auction.</p><p>“I’m donating the gear I use in the game so that it can be auctioned off and given back to the community and to Kumamoto itself,” Murakami said. “Personally, I will do a charity myself. In the upcoming days, I will be able to present that.”</p><p>• Right-hander Drew Thorpe (Tommy John surgery) had an impressive rehab outing Thursday for Double-A Birmingham, throwing four innings of one-hit ball with five strikeouts. In fact, since he only threw 43 pitches, Thorpe had to finish his work in the bullpen. entries.title: Shota Imanaga pitches well, but Cubs blanked by Yankees
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> left-hander Shota Imanaga understood the challenge the Yankees posed, even with Aaron Judge, Giancarlo Stanton and Cody Bellinger sidelined.</p><p>He did his part. The Cubs just didn’t give him the run support he needed.</p><p>Imanaga allowed two home runs in what otherwise was a terrific start, and the Cubs were shut out for the 10th time in a 2-0 loss Friday to the Yankees at Wrigley Field.</p><p>‘‘He’s been fantastic,’’ outfielder Ian Happ said of Imanaga. ‘‘The ability to throw a splitter competitively quite a bit and what he’s been able to do to lefties with that sinker, it’s been fun to watch. Not enough run support for him today, but he was fantastic.’’</p><p>After taking three of four games from the Cardinals in St. Louis, the Cubs were shut down by right-hander Will Warren and two relievers. They managed five hits in dropping the opener of the weekend series.</p><p>Imanaga, who was coming off scoreless outings in victories against the Twins and Pirates, was a tough-luck loser. He allowed two runs and four hits in 6 2/3 innings and struck out six without a walk.</p><p>Imanaga (7-9) gave up a long homer to Amed Rosario in the fourth and a drive to Spencer Jones in the fifth. But he didn’t get the support this time after the Cubs combined to outscore the Twins and Pirates 21-1 in his previous two starts.</p><p>‘‘I feel like right now I’m thinking about a lot of things where I had come up with a game plan against their hitters [and] the hitters come up with a game plan against me,’’ Imanaga said through an interpreter. ‘‘Do I go with my game plan or see what they’re doing and make those adjustments according to what they seem like their game plan is? And just thinking about what adjustments I need to do for each start or each inning.’’</p><p>Warren (8-5) held the Cubs to four hits in 6 2/3 innings. He struck out seven, walked none and retired 12 batters in a row before Alex Bregman and Happ chased him with back-to-back singles in the seventh. Paul Blackburn got Nico Hoerner to ground into a force to end that threat.</p><p>Pedro Ramirez singled with one out in the ninth against David Bednar, but Michael Busch flied out and Bregman grounded out to end the game.</p><p>Imanaga retired the first 11 batters he faced before Rosario launched a 450-foot drive to center. Jones made it 2-0 with a drive to right an inning later. Imanaga has allowed 24 homers this season.</p><p>Imanaga left to cheers in the seventh after retiring Trent Grisham on a fly ball for the second out.</p><p>Tyler Ferguson then got three outs before exiting with two on in the eighth. Maine East graduate Antoine Kelly, making his major-league debut after being called up from Triple-A Iowa, struck out slugger Ben Rice to end that threat and pitched around a walk in the ninth.</p><p>Kelly said he only had his parents, girlfriend, uncle and agent on hand, rather than a large group of friends and family, because ‘‘it was so last-minute.’’</p><p>He also admitted he wasn’t a Cubs or White Sox fan growing up. His team? entries.title: 1 dead in wrong-way Dan Ryan Expy. crash
entries.summary: <p>One person died and two others were critically injured Friday evening when a wrong-way driver caused a five-vehicle crash on the Dan Ryan Expressway, Illinois State Police said. </p><p>A southbound driver entered the northbound express lanes of I-94 near 31st Street and crashed about three miles south near Garfield Boulevard around 5:50 p.m., the state police said in a statement. </p><p>State police said one person was pronounced dead. Two others were taken to hospitals in critical condition, according to a Chicago Fire Department spokesperson.</p><p>Northbound traffic was being diverted off at 67th Street, state police said.</p>

entries.title: Review: It's Finn Wolfhard's first Lolla, but he's no stranger to Chicago
entries.summary: <p>With memories still fresh from Djo’s Lolla love fest in 2025, another “Stranger Things” star tried to fill the gap on Friday – albeit, with a very different style of music. Finn Wolfhard — known for playing character Mike Wheeler — made his real-life solo festival debut here in Chicago, which makes sense when you consider the city has become a special spot in his music career.</p><p>Wolfhard’s 2025 debut “Happy Birthday” was recorded in town with co-producer Kai Slater and instrumentalists Asher Case and Isaac Lowenstein (all from the local band Lifeguard) as well as Sofia Jensen from Chicago’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/music/2025/03/27/free-range-fronted-by-gifted-chicago-songwriter-sofia-jensen-is-growing-up" target="_blank" ><u>Free Range</u></a>. “Happy Birthday” and its quick follow-up, “Fire from the Hip,” which was just released July 10, also feature the handiwork of Twin Peaks guitarist Cadien Lake James, who has long been Wolfhard’s mentor. There’s also a sub-context to the young talent’s music: his great love of Chicago titans Wilco.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure Wolfhard’s material, though it may not have landed as well at Lollapalooza as it would have at, say, Evanston Folk Fest. The audience motility suggested as much. Wolfhard at one point suggested they “jump around a little.” What started with a crowded house and ear-piercing fangirl screaming at the top of the set was nearly muted by the end as most of the devotees thinned out, on to the next high-energy romp.</p><p>Wolfhard’s music has its place. It’s a beautiful slow-burner assortment chock full of electric and acoustic whimsy and layered with keys, lap steel, fiddle and drums from six additional skilled musicians. His foot-stomping and guitar-whipping are fun to watch, too, and he’s just as versatile when he drops an instrument.</p><p>This is not the Canadian’s first rodeo, either. The now 23-year-old began his musical pursuits when he was just 14 with the power pop band Calpurnia and then moved into the indie rock vein with The Aubreys. In addition to Wilco, he’s also a fan of the Rolling Stones, which informed much of his new material, as heard on the rousing opener “I’ll Let You Finish.” In his Lolla set, he covered another oldie but goodie with Faces’ “Ooh La La.” It also may be notable to mention that Wolfhard is working on a biopic of The Replacements. entries.title: Review: Slayyyter finds her best Worst self at Lollapalooza
entries.summary: <p>From a Midwest Princess to Midwest Pleb, Lollapalooza has really cornered the market on catching regional hype stars in the moment, starting with Chappell Roan in 2024 and, this year, Slayyyter.</p><p>In a repeat last-minute pivot this week, organizers smartly promoted the electro pop artist — alter ego of St. Louis native Catherine Grace Garner — to a main stage in anticipation of the large draw. A majority of the park did mosey over, proudly donning pairs of bunny ears and trucker caps, both familiar talismans in Slayyyter’s diabolical music videos as of late. Garner had her own pick, a bedazzled cap that spelled out Slayyyterpalooza. No truer words ever spoken.</p><p>“I always wanted to play Lollapalooza, and I’m so happy we’re doing this today y’all,” she remarked about making her festival debut. “I want to thank you for coming to my set. Everything happening with me lately is so crazy, and you all make me feel like I’m such a celebrity. It’s like I’m actually kind of famous,” she added.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b90000" name="image-b90000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/56ed8da/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F6a%2F82%2Fc469c1d74584bf396a01f69f3ed8%2Flollapicsday2-260731-06.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ab76eea/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F6a%2F82%2Fc469c1d74584bf396a01f69f3ed8%2Flollapicsday2-260731-06.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/399e6a2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F6a%2F82%2Fc469c1d74584bf396a01f69f3ed8%2Flollapicsday2-260731-06.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Slayyyter performs on the Bud Light stage on Day 2 of Lollapalooza in Grant Park, Friday, July 31, 2026. It’s also her first album ever to pop up in top spots on Billboard charts after years of hustling to make it with a self-titled mixtape in 2019, a proper debut album “Troubled Paradise” in 2021 and 2023’s “Starf---er.” There was nothing amiss with any of the records — each of them cast a net of Y2k pop girlie gold; one track, “Daddy AF,” landed in the Oscar-winning “Anora.” But the output just wasn’t different enough from the crowded pop milieu to break out.</p><p>With “Wor$t Girl,” Garner has found her best self. entries.title: White Sox looking a lot like Rays, and that's not by accident
entries.summary: <p>ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> fans of a certain age must cringe every time their team visits Tropicana Field. They know the ballpark, which opened in 1990 as the Florida Suncoast Dome, was built to lure the Sox, who were trying to cut a deal for a new stadium in the late 80s.</p><p>But on June 30, 1988 — or July 1, depending on whether you believe the late Gov. Jim Thompson could suspend time — chairman Jerry Reinsdorf and the Sox got the financing for New Comiskey Park. And the rest is history.</p><p>But in 2026, the Sox no longer want to play where the Rays play. They want to play how the Rays play.</p><p>That’s not a bad idea, considering the Rays have two more postseason appearances than the Sox (11-9) in about, oh, 100 fewer years of existence. But let’s not nitpick. The Rays have the best record in the American League and a payroll in the bottom third. That sounds like a business model the perennially frugal Sox can get behind.</p><p>And they have. General manager Chris Getz has been looking at how teams such as the Rays and Brewers, both largely frugal themselves, succeed. That effort included poaching former Rays executive Carlos Rodriguez, who spent more than 15 seasons in the organization, and naming him an assistant general manager.</p><p>It also has included bringing in former Rays players, such as Tanner Murray, Everson Pereira and Tristan Peters. Their connection to the Rays isn’t the only reason Getz wanted them, but it certainly didn’t hurt.</p><p>Peters has been the most productive of the bunch, flashing enough leather and power to earn an All-Star bid in his rookie season. He isn’t sure whether the Sox are being influenced by the Rays’ way, but definitely sees similarities in the teams.</p><p>“Kind of the same play style. I think we have more slug,” Peters told the Sun-Times. “They’re bunting; we bunt, or we’ve got that small ball. Just that grit factor; they’ve got that, too. I know some of the guys on the team. They’re ballers; they’re good people, too. Similar team.”</p><p>Peters learned with the Rays what the Sox want for themselves, some of which they already have developed with this group.</p><p>“How to play as a team,” Peters said. “How to really mesh with your teammates and really play for them and win, too. I think that’s the culture here. We’re playing for each other. And I think I’ve learned that coming from there. It’s a very similar culture.”</p><p>The Rays even speak a similar language. The Sox break down hitting into three elements: decisions, contact and damage. Peters said the Rays have what they call “pillars,” which happen to be decisions, contact and damage.</p><p>“That’s how you’re evaluated in the minor leagues,” he said. “So, yeah, it’s very similar the way that their player development is, too, from what I’ve experienced anyway.”</p><p>To be sure, Peters played in only four games for the Rays, in 2025. But after being drafted by the Brewers in 2021 — out of Southern Illinois — he joined the Rays’ Double-A team in 2023 and played for their Triple-A team the next two years. He was indoctrinated in the Rays’ way.</p><p>Getz would like to instill many of those lessons in the Sox. Under manager Will Venable, some already have. entries.title: If you could perform on any stage in Chicago, which one would you choose? Here's what you told us
entries.summary: <p>We asked readers to tell us which stage in Chicago they'd perform on if they could pick any one. Here's what you told us, lightly edited for clarity:</p><p>"Pritzker Pavilion. I watched it being built while learning to be a 'musician.' Many great performances I've witnessed on that stage."<br><i>— Daniel R. Shaughnessy</i></p><p>"The Hideout, just to get one of those epic introductions."<br><i>— Darin Latimer</i></p><p>"I’d love to be on the stage at the Lyric Opera. It’d be a priceless memory."<br><i>— Paul Lockwood</i></p><p>"Huntington Bank Pavilion at Northerly Island — intimate, and the view!"<br><i>— Topher Menard</i></p><p>"Just east of the parking garage for the Cook County Courts along California Boulevard sits Plaza Garibaldi. bidding wars for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/01/30/affordability-chicago-housing-market-homebuyers-experts-economists" >few homes hitting the market</a>, especially in neighborhoods like Lake View, Lincoln Park and Northalsted. The battle among buyers has been great for home sellers as properties sell for up to hundreds of thousands of dollars over their asking price. And some buyers — to help sweeten the deal — have been waiving certain contingencies like inspections.</p><p>“Things have been crazy. January was really the start of it, and things just went kind of nutso from there,” Alley Ballard, broker with real estate firm @properties, said.</p><p>Neighborhoods with strong retail corridors, like Andersonville, Lincoln Park and Wicker Park, are seeing high demand, Ballard said. But across the city, she’s seen homes sell for $100,000 to $200,000 — sometimes even $300,000 — above their asking price.</p><p>Zillow data shows Chicago's housing market started the year hot, when it's typically a slow period for home sales.<b> </b>An April report said 25% of Chicago homes in February sold in seven days or less, illustrating the speed at which properties flew off the market. And 24.7% of February's home sale prices were above asking. For homes in the 60657 ZIP code, which covers Lake View, Lake View East and Roscoe Village 63.4% of homes sold above its list price, and more than half, or 53%, sold in seven days or less.</p><p>“Chicago is still too fast relative to the rest of the country and because homes that come on the market still sell so rapidly, inventory is not building fast enough,” Orphe Divounguy, senior economist at Zillow, said.</p><h3>‘Lot of competition’</h3><p>Agents said they don’t see the bidding wars ending soon, as the lack of new inventory remains an issue.</p><p>The number of new listings in June was down 11.3% year-over-year for single-family homes in Chicago and 2.8% for attached properties, like condos and townhomes, according to the Chicago Association of Realtors. There were 1,245 new single-family homes listed last month and 2,083 attached homes, the association found.</p><p>Meanwhile, the number of homes for sale hit a historical low in June. There were 1,373 single-family homes and 2,121 attached properties on the market — the lowest figures the association has on record since 2008, the start of its available data. That's less than two months of supply for both attached and detached properties, well below the 4-6 month threshold needed for a housing market to be considered balanced.</p><p>“This year, we have all of those prospective home buyers that have been trying to purchase homes the last four or five years coming out of COVID but have lost multi-offer situations. Combine that with the new rush of buyers out there that wants to move for the usual reasons and with the limited inventory, it really creates a lot of competition," Sammy Lubeck, Realtor at Baird & Warner, said. </p><p>Years of high interest rates following the pandemic kept many prospective homebuyers on the sidelines, but agents said buyers are feeling restless, spurring demand. But borrowing costs are still high. The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rose to 6.66% from 6.58% last week, Freddie Mac said Thursday. It's now the highest since July 31, 2025, when the rate was 6.72%. In February, the rate fell to 5.98% — the lowest since 2022.</p><p>Divounguy said although there have been more home sales in Chicago over the past year, it's still below pre-pandemic levels. That's because there aren't enough homes on the market, and once listed, they're selling fast.</p><p>"Unless we get enough listings on the market, the market's going to remain tight, and that keeps the pressure on prices and rents," Divounguy said. "Chicago prices and rents are still rising relatively faster than other major markets."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-5b0000" name="html-embed-module-5b0000"></a><div style="min-height:472px" id="datawrapper-vis-GcImm"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/GcImm/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-GcImm"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/GcImm/full.png" alt="Home costs on the rise in north side neighborhoods (Line chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>In Lincoln Park and Lake View, the average sale price for a home has risen dramatically following the pandemic. The average sale price for Lincoln Park properties in June was $795,000, up 12% from June 2025 when the average sales price was $710,000, according to Zillow's InfoSparks. In Lake View, the average sale price in June was $587,500 — a 5.4% year-over-year increase from $557,500.</p><p>Homes in Lincoln Park and Lake View sold in an average of 17 and 23 days, respectively. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-f00000" name="html-embed-module-f00000"></a><div style="min-height:472px" id="datawrapper-vis-nZIyb"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/nZIyb/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-nZIyb"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/nZIyb/full.png" alt="With low supply, homes are selling fast (Line chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>“It's a frenzy because there's so little inventory,” Dawn McKenna, broker and founding principal of Dawn McKenna Group, said.</p><p>McKenna said Lincoln Park is currently one of the best markets in Chicago. Her team listed a two-bedroom, two-bathroom<b> </b>property with a roofdeck in April for $1 million. There were 17 offers, and it sold in May<b> </b>for $1.2 million, she said.</p><p>“If something is really great — it's a great location, and it's priced where the market is meeting the demand — it just pops off,” McKenna said. “Lincoln Park is the hottest market. entries.title: Dear Abby: Long-suffering wife and mother is ready to move on
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am living in total dysfunction with my daughter (32) and husband (75). I am retired and going on 76. My daughter will not work and is controlling my life. She has OCD and refuses medication. It's so bad that she has become completely dependent on me. She makes me drive her and yells at me while I do. If she doesn't get her way, she yells and calls me horrible names. The police have been called to the house in the past, but it only made things worse for me.</p><p>She has been accepted to a college with a partial scholarship for her second master's degree and wants me to fund her housing. Her father, who is also verbally abusive, leaves home before she gets up and comes home around 8. He then sits in the driveway to avoid her. I have been abandoned to deal with her.</p><p>Abby, I taught school for 40 years, raised three kids and did all the work around here while he worked a cushy job for his parents. I also found on his phone that he has a girlfriend. I am so upset living with him that I want out of this house and away from him.</p><p>I daydream of getting my own apartment and living alone. If I file for divorce, my husband will go after my pension. He has no retirement savings and still works. What can I do? — <i>UGLY SITUATION</i></p><p><b>DEAR SITUATION:</b> Talk to a lawyer! Have you done so? Your assumption that your pension isn't safe may not be true, and a good attorney may be able to help protect it.</p><p>Additionally, I urge you to call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233 right away. Even though no one has been physically violent, you are still a victim of emotional (and possibly financial) abuse. No one should have to live under the conditions you have described.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I recently found out that the state removed all of my good friend's children and placed them into protective custody. I got this information from a local news website I was browsing one day. She is being charged with multiple felony counts of child neglect. I knew she didn't have custody of her kids prior to finding the article, but she never mentioned to me what was really going on. This woman has been like a sister to me for years.</p><p>I'm torn about how to feel. I have yet to tell her I know the true situation. We haven't spoken since I found out. Do I reach out and ask for her side of things? The article laid out that the neglect had been occurring for years. I feel awful that I never knew how bad it truly was for her kids. Part of me wants to ask what is going on; another part wants to disconnect from her forever. — <i>MAY NEVER KNOW THE TRUTH</i></p><p><b>DEAR MAY:</b> What have you to gain by contacting this woman and telling her you know the situation? The story has been all over the media, and she likely assumes that everyone knows about it. If, in light of your long relationship, you feel you would like to be supportive, then reach out to her. However, if you're merely curious, then listen to your gut and step out of the picture.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p><p>To receive a collection of Abby's most memorable — and most frequently requested — poems and essays, send your name and mailing address, plus check or money order for $8 (U.S. funds), to: Dear Abby — Keepers Booklet, P.O. Box 446, Kings Mills, OH 45034-0446. (Shipping and handling are included in the price.)</p>

entries.title: Durbin must reject sneaky move to expand ICE authority
entries.summary: <p>“We must rein in ICE abuses before another life is lost,” Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., <a class="Link" href="https://www.durbin.senate.gov/newsroom/press-releases/durbin-statement-on-fatal-ice-officer-shootings-in-houston-and-maine" target="_blank" >said last month</a> after two fathers, <a class="Link" href="https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/nation/2026/07/25/lorenzo-salgado-araujo-van-drugs-houston-ice/91050215007/" target="_blank" >Lorenzo Salgado Araujo</a> in Houston and <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/07/15/us/joan-sebastian-guerrero-ice-shooting-maine" target="_blank" >Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero</a>, in Maine, were shot and killed by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers.</p><p>Most Americans <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/poll-nearly-two-thirds-of-americans-say-ice-has-gone-too-far-in-immigration-crackdown" target="_blank" >agree with Durbin’s sentiment </a>that ICE is out of control, and so do many of his colleagues in Congress. Not a single Democrat voted to hand more funds to the Department of Homeland Security in June. </p><p>So it is alarming that Durbin has thrown his weight behind another bill, the Combating Organized Retail Crime Act, or “<a class="Link" href="https://thehill.com/opinion/congress-blog/homeland-security/5941947-combating-crime-act-backlash/" target="_blank" >CORCA</a>," which would empower DHS and ICE to collect data on American shoppers and expand the reach of immigration enforcement into our communities.</p><p>The retail industry has <a class="Link" href="https://www.grassley.senate.gov/news/news-releases/law-enforcement-and-retail-industry-leaders-call-on-congress-to-pass-the-combating-organized-retail-crime-act-through-the-ndaa" target="_blank" >lobbied heavily</a> in support, winning bipartisan support from members of Congress who are afraid of being painted as “soft” on crime. However, after learning about the expansion of ICE’s power in this bill, 10 Democratic House co-sponsors ultimately decided not to vote in favor. Now, the bill is being readied for debate in the U.S. Senate. </p><p>Knowing that the bill is indefensible on its merits, the retail lobby is going into overdrive to sneak it into the National Defense Authorization Act, a must-pass legislative package. The lobby has published op-eds across the country attempting to <a class="Link" href="https://www.northjersey.com/story/opinion/2026/07/07/cargo-theft-costs-nj-millions-sen-booker-must-back-reforms-opinion/90822554007/?gnt-cfr=1&gca-cat=p&gca-uir=true&gca-epti=z11xx67p004250l004450c004250e1182xxv11xx67d--55--b--55--&gca-ft=189&gca-ds=sophi" target="_blank" >pressure New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker,</a> who has long been opposed to CORCA, as well as<a class="Link" href="https://www.providencejournal.com/story/opinion/columns/2026/07/18/why-cargo-theft-is-costing-you-more-at-the-store-opinion/90882310007/?gnt-cfr=1&gca-cat=p&gca-uir=false&gca-epti=z11----p002350l002950c002350u113017e003400v116217o11----&gca-ft=40&gca-ds=sophi" target="_blank" ><u> </u>Rhode Island Sen. Jack Reed</a>.</p><p>Durbin has been a lead co-sponsor of CORCA and approved moving it quickly and without debate on the National Defense Authorization Act. We call on him and other Democratic senators to reject this bill and continue to lead in the fight to rein in ICE.</p><p>A broad coalition of over <a class="Link" href="https://drive.google.com/file/d/1-L-BwH-bWChX7tGpew9EFSfHzoK95_cT/view" target="_blank" >130 civil rights, criminal justice reform and immigration groups</a> — including the NAACP, American Civil Liberties Union and others — are urging senators to instead focus on real solutions to keep Americans safe.</p><p>Durbin has been a vocal opponent of expanding immigration enforcement, including voting against the Laken Riley Act, which increased ICE’s detention authority and which many senators have come to regret supporting. As civil rights leaders, we urge him now to call for CORCA to be debated on its own merits and to vote no.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.vera.org/people/insha-rahman" target="_blank" ><i>Insha Rahman</i></a><i>, president, Vera Action</i> <br><a class="Link" href="https://www.nilc.org/people/kica-matos/" target="_blank" ><i>Kica Matos</i></a><i>, president, National Immigration Law Center</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-930000" name="module-930000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Unaccompanied children lose legal counsel</h3><p>Legal service providers, representing nearly <a class="Link" href="https://acaciajustice.org/leaders-call-out-trump-administrations-move-to-strip-unaccompanied-children-of-legal-counsel/" target="_blank" >20,000 unaccompanied children</a> across the country, were just defunded by the federal government. This means that children will be forced to appear before an immigration judge alone.</p><p>While observing a Chicago immigration courtroom, I saw 12-year-old “Carlos," standing before an immigration judge. Carlos’ attorney told the judge that Carlos' father went through the government’s vetting process to have his son released but was detained and deported — a practice the Trump administration has adopted to meet its mass deportation quotas and to get children to “voluntarily” leave the country. Kids are used as bait, and parents obviously come forward hoping to reunite. Who wouldn’t?</p><p>Six months later, Carlos and his attorney came back to court. The detention center Carlos was placed in was shutting down. His move to a new facility was imminent. This would partly restart vetting and further delay Carlos’ release or lead to his deportation.</p><p>Carlos’ attorney asked for one more extension. The attorney for the government argued against the extension, but the judge granted just another week.</p><p>One week later, Carlos was released to his aunt, a U.S. citizen. The judge was visibly relieved. </p><p>One child’s life. One family’s drama. Just another day in court with detained kids.</p><p>Imagine if Carlos hadn’t had an attorney to advocate for him?</p><p>Trump is dismantling the network of nearly 100 legal service providers representing unaccompanied kids like Carlos. The contract to represent these kids, a bipartisan program funded since 2003, came to an end July 31. </p><p>Now tens of thousands of children face the possibility of representing themselves in court. Do you know a 12-year-old? This is just wrong.</p><p><i>Joy Olson, Milwaukee</i></p><h3>Read up on 1919 race riot</h3><p>Thank you to the Sun-Times for printing the article headlined <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/other-views/2026/07/24/1919-chicago-race-riot-commemoration-project-peter-cole-franklin-dunni-cosey-gay-myles-francis" target="_blank" >“Remembering victims of 1919 Chicago race riot: 38 names set in stone</a>" on July 25. This is an important historical event, and it is fitting that it was memorialized by these stone markers.</p><p>For those who want to learn more, I highly recommend the 2018 book <a class="Link" href="https://www.abebooks.com/9780358667995/Few-Red-Drops-Chicago-Race-0358667992/plp" target="_blank" >“A Few Red Drops: The Chicago Race Riot of 1919"</a> by Claire Hartfield. The book examines the events in great detail and includes many pictures — some of which are hard to view because of their stark reality. </p><p>Historical parallels between 1919 and today are worth noting: The author explains that tensions that fueled the riot had been building for decades. Waves of white immigrants from Europe and Black migrants from the South converged to form an underclass divided by racial prejudice. This racial animus was exploited by the tycoons who controlled the labor market by pitting these groups against one another.</p><p>This situation sounds all too familiar, does it not? Today we have Latino immigrants pitted against the white working class, a situation that continues to be fully exploited by Donald Trump and his supporters. </p><p>And that is why we must never forget these events. We risk repeating the same costly mistakes, to our great detriment as a society.</p><p><i>Bob Chimis, Elmwood Park</i></p><h3>City made flooding worse</h3><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/other-views/2026/07/27/flooding-act-of-god-rundown-infrastructure-sewers-drainage-catherine-nakalembe" >Catherine Nakalembe</a> is right — Chicago’s flooding is a policy failure, not an act of God. I would go further. In some neighborhoods, the city is actively destroying the sewers it's supposed to maintain.</p><p>I am a retired city of Chicago sewer engineer. This summer I had 15 inches of water gushing out of my floor drain and 18 inches of sewage in my basement. I hired and paid a private contractor to televise my drain line to find out why.</p><p>The Department of Water Management had installed a new water main on our block. To meet water and sewer separation standards, the crew replaced the private drains with ductile iron pipe. But instead of reconnecting my drain where it had always been, they reconnected it 8 feet upstream of the original connection, against the flow of the main sewer. My house is now a relief valve for the main sewer. That is what gushed up through my floor drain.</p><p>It did not stop at my property. At our alderperson's request, the main sewer was televised as well. That report shows broken pipe and voids beneath the street: new damage to a 100-year-old, 12-inch main sewer that was undersized before anyone touched it.</p><p>Requests to correct it have gone nowhere. My drain was dug up twice before being repaired to code.</p><p>The fix is not complicated, just expensive. Put the connections back where they belong and repair what was broken by replacing the failing and inadequate 12-inch sewer main with oversized reinforced pipe, 24 to 36 inches. </p><p>In my city career, we required private developers to detain their storm-surge water. The city should hold itself to that same standard and use oversized pipe to hold the storm surge under the street instead of in our basements. </p><p>I live two blocks from a Deep Tunnel drop shaft. More capacity in the neighborhood pipes would buy that water the time it needs to get to the drop shaft.</p><p>Blaming God is convenient. Blaming the weather is convenient. Neither one is responsible for my basement flooding.</p><p><i>Edward Koehler, Ravenswood</i></p><h3>Under the weather</h3><p>I'm sure thousands of American victims of floods, fires and tornadoes are content knowing that President Donald Trump and most Republicans believe that climate change is just a "woke" hoax.</p><p><i>Robert Kleps, Oak Park</i></p><h3>Highlight Medicaid, Medicare’s value</h3><p>At a time when healthcare through Medicaid and Medicare is under constant siege, I hope you will continue to print letters, like <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/letters-to-the-editor/2026/07/22/never-underestimate-medicare-value-property-tax-assessments-errors-global-warming" >Lequita Michelle Mayhew’s recent writeup</a> in support of those beneficial and often lifesaving programs.</p><p>After 40 years of private insurance in the often topsy-turvy corporate world, I was able to retire and enroll in Medicare. The stability and peace of mind knowing I am covered are benefits that I couldn't appreciate until I was in it and in need of care. In the past, I never knew if my employer would change insurers, if those companies would raise rates or if my employer would decide to save money by reducing their contribution.</p><p>Based on my experience and many others, I believe the time has come for a national single-payer healthcare system. Many will scream "but my taxes," but once they realize the net benefits, they will not want to go back.</p><p><i>John Hankes, Streeterville</i></p><h3>Joliet Treatment Center’s plight unacceptable</h3><p>What determines whether a society has become morally bankrupt? I’m not an expert, so I can't say for sure. However, the investigation by the Marshall Project, Sun-Times and WBEZ of the conditions at the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/07/24/joliet-prison-fires-mental-health-illinois-department-corrections" >Joliet Treatment Center</a> is quite a clear-cut case that we are far from where we need to be. When prisoners are so desperate for help that the only way they believe they will receive such assistance is to light their cells and themselves on fire, all of us should be disgusted.</p><p>Instead of bemoaning a higher property tax, what if we allowed those increased funds to help the Joliet Treatment Center? Is it more important that we maintain the lifestyles, or should we demand that people who are invisible to society not be discarded so carelessly, no matter the cost?</p><p>I find it both odd and dispiriting that we collectively accept that perhaps the most vulnerable population — prisoners with severe mental health problems — are living under such horrific conditions. </p><p>If we need a selfish reason to safeguard the lives of these inmates, we should consider that by ensuring that they are always treated as humans, we are guaranteeing that the rest of us will not become invisible. This shameful moral failure is our responsibility, yet I doubt that we as a society will fulfill our obligations to provide the most basic human needs to the inmates of the Joliet Treatment Center. If this isn’t a sign of the moral rot at the center of our society, I truly don’t know what is.</p><p><i>Ethan Feingold, Lake View</i> </p><h3>Cold comfort</h3><p>Recalling spells like our recent scorching heat waves, I salute and sympathize with all the laborers who work outside. For the roofers, road gangs, landscapers, construction workers and others, there's no way around such weather — only through it. That's a toughness I haven't had to match since my competitive running days. Luckily for them, off hours offer relief indoors.</p><p>Not so during the Great Depression. Mom said that for the roughest times before air conditioning became an assumption and home was an oven, the family would soak bedsheets in cool water to wrap in before retiring to the yard for the night. Others dragged out their mattresses or headed for the Chicago parks. And after the heat broke, it might take another three days for building interiors to cool down.</p><p>That was then, but even now our Polish-born housekeeper tells me most European housing lacks the priceless appliance we call AC.</p><p>So who do the rest of us thank for this underrated blessing? An early 20th century engineer named <a class="Link" href="https://www.williscarrier.com/" target="_blank" >Willis Carrier</a>. Probably not 1 in 10 people know this, but without him the human comfort level periodically falls clear off the table. And yet even in his native New York state, he's nearly forgotten. Certainly not by me, though. Every time I walk in from an outside inferno to my temperature-controlled digs, I send positive thoughts along to Mr. C., wherever he is today.</p><p><i>Tom Gregg, Niles </i></p><h3></h3>

entries.title: Diversity is good for business, report on Black consumer spending finds
entries.summary: <p>When a brand reduces its commitment to diversity, equity and inclusion, Black consumers respond with their wallets.</p><p>The National Urban League's 2026 State of Black America report, <a class="Link" href="https://stateofblackamerica.org/reports/2026" target="_blank" >“America 250: Is The American Dream Dead?”</a> includes a special section on Black consumer behavior and spending. "<a class="Link" href="https://stateofblackamerica.org/special-section/2026" target="_blank" >The Why Behind the Buy: Analyzing Black Buying Power</a>" segment finds that Black consumers are spending more, engaging more deeply with brands and exercising greater influence across major sectors of the economy than many companies recognize. </p><p>But they are demanding something in return: authenticity, respect and a genuine commitment to inclusion.</p><p>At a time when some corporations are retreating from DEI commitments in response to political pressure, Black consumers are paying attention. The study found that Black consumers are highly likely to reduce spending or seek alternatives when companies scale back their commitments to diversity and inclusion.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d60000" name="module-d60000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>That finding should serve as a wake-up call for companies that view inclusion as a public relations exercise rather than a business strategy. Consumers increasingly expect corporations to reflect the diversity of the country they serve. They want to see fairness, representation and cultural relevance embedded in products, services, marketing and corporate behavior.</p><p>Loyalty, the research makes clear, is earned through authenticity and lost without it.</p><p>The report’s main recommendations:<br></p><ol class="rte2-style-ol" id="rte-f85cf331-8c66-11f1-b9cd-277944a8655a" start="1"><li>Treat Black consumers as a growth segment. Spend levels already justify dedicated investment.<br></li><li>Make authenticity a brand commitment. It drives loyalty and carries real revenue risk if abandoned.<br></li><li>Close the supply gap for Black-owned and culturally aligned products. Especially in beauty and finance.<br></li><li>Prioritize youth-first, creator-led channels. Ages 18–34 and 35–54 are the consistent growth engine.<br></li><li>Lead with trust over influence. Peer pressure is a weaker driver than assumed.</li></ol><p>The report challenges long-standing stereotypes about Black consumer behavior. Black consumers are not simply followers of trends or influencers. In fact, social influence ranks relatively low among the factors driving purchasing decisions. Instead, Black consumers place a premium on authenticity and respect. They reward brands that demonstrate a genuine understanding of their experiences and values. They reject those that engage in superficial outreach.</p><p>In financial services, the research shows Black consumers display high levels of financial confidence and a strong desire to build wealth. Yet traditional wealth-building products continue to underserve them. While banking participation has largely reached parity, gaps remain in retirement investment and wealth accumulation. </p><p>The opportunity is enormous for institutions willing to meet consumers where they are with accessible products, relevant education and digital-first tools.</p><p>In health and wellness, Black consumers are increasingly seeking culturally relevant products and services that acknowledge their unique needs and experiences. The lesson for providers and businesses is straightforward: Culturally competent care is not just good practice; it is smart economics.</p><p>The same pattern emerges in beauty, travel and retail. Black consumers consistently express a desire for products, experiences and brands that reflect their identities and aspirations. Yet many industries continue to underserve this demand. The result is a gap between consumer expectations and marketplace offerings, one that innovative businesses should move quickly to close.</p><p>For generations, Black Americans have contributed disproportionately to American culture, innovation and economic growth while receiving disproportionately little investment in return. Despite these barriers, Black consumers continue to shape markets, influence trends and create new opportunities for economic expansion.</p><p>The National Urban League has long argued that equity and economic growth are not competing goals. They are mutually reinforcing. This report provides powerful evidence that when businesses invest in understanding and serving Black consumers, everyone benefits. Stronger businesses, stronger communities and a stronger economy all flow from the same principle: Inclusion drives growth.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/authors/marc-h-morial" target="_blank" ><i>Marc H. Morial</i></a><i> is president and CEO of the National Urban League</i> <i>and</i> <i>was mayor of New Orleans from 1994 to 2002.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-810000" name="module-810000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. entries.title: Chicago teens riff on 'Love Island,' 'aura' trend to pitch campaigns pushing peers to put down guns
entries.summary: <p>Dozens of nervous teens packed a downtown conference room this week to pitch a panel of city officials and civic leaders on social media campaigns they’ve spent the summer developing.</p><p>The messaging of their campaigns was the same: get teens to put down their guns.</p><p>But they took different approaches.</p><p>One team riffed on the slang term “aura,” used by members of Generation Alpha to describe someone’s vibe, as a way to convince their peers that there’s nothing cool about guns.</p><p>Other teams borrowed from the popular reality dating show “Love Island” to present skits in which “islanders” voted out participants who owned guns.</p><p>But it was a campaign called <a class="Link" href="https://www.canva.com/design/DAHQxzdklLk/yCimBXg1veHL7Wute2klYA/edit" target="_blank" ><u>T.R.A.P.</u></a> that emerged victorious on Thursday. It urged teens not to fall for the trap of believing that they’d be safer with a gun, citing research that shows firearm owners are more likely to get shot.</p><p>One of their “spring cleaning” skits depicted teens cleaning out their rooms at the behest of their parents, tossing out everything from old clothes to guns.</p><p>Judge Cherie Animashaun, founder of the Her Rising Initiative, said she circled the T.R.A.P. team’s name in her notebook as soon as they took to the podium.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure So for them to use something that I think our community has heard time and time again, but to reclaim it, it's just so cool.”</p><p>A six-week summer program organized by the nonprofit Project Unloaded recruits teens from the South and West sides of the city, many of whom have seen the toll of gun violence up close.</p><p>Luis Delgado, a member of the T.R.A.P. team, said he almost lost one of his relatives to gun violence several years back.</p><p>“Thank the Lord that they ended up surviving it, but it was such a scary moment,” the 17-year-old recalled. “We didn’t know if they were going to live or not, and that just sparked something in our family that we wanted to get guns away from the household.”</p><p>During the program, Delgado and other teens got a crash course in how to develop a social media campaign from scratch.</p><p>They met with advertising experts who helped them shape their ideas. They produced their own reels and skits. And they even developed prototypes of merchandise for their campaigns, from t-shirts to travel mugs and totebags.</p><p>Though the program was paid, Delgado said, “I could care less about the money. It was more about making an impact in my community.”</p><p>Delgado said he talked about the T.R.A.P. campaign with his friends, sharing the videos his team filmed and the gun violence facts they learned throughout the program. Were the friends we lost to gun violence safer with a gun?’”</p><p>“It didn't just take me one day. It took a week, a week and a half to talk with them … to annoy them basically with the facts, statistics, and show them that you can let go of guns because no one's gonna judge you. By letting go of a gun, you are showing courage that a lot of people sometimes just don't have.”</p><p>Kamari Markiyah Brown, from Lawndale, said she was set on buying her own gun before she joined Project Unloaded.</p><p>“I felt unsafe, especially with what's happening to young Black teens like myself,” she said.</p><p>She changed her mind after she learned through the program that having a gun at home increases the risk of suicide.</p><p>“Now that I know that,” she said, "I do not want anything to do with a gun.”</p><p>Brown said the program has changed how she perceives her neighborhood and the world around her.</p><p>“I knew the world was unsafe, but I didn't realize it was to this extent,” she said. “But I also didn't realize how much effect I could have on my peers.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/public-safety/2026/06/05/scooter-escooters-lane-tech-safety-teenagers-crashes" target="_blank" >For Chicago teens, e-scooters are fun, convenient but sometimes dangerous, even deadly</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: How we photographed the aftermath of basketball coach Tim Bankston's shooting
entries.summary: <p>This week’s top photo comes from Visual Journalist <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/candace-chambers" target="_blank" >Candace Dane Chambers</a>.</p><h3><b>What makes this photo important?</b></h3><p>Former South Side basketball star and current beloved high school coach Tim Bankston was found shot dead in an Auburn Gresham home on Wednesday morning. Bankston’s community impact spanned decades, first making waves as the Simeon Academy point guard who led the high school to a 1984 state championship. Bankston began coaching at Thornton Fractional North High School in 2002 and was inducted into the Illinois Basketball Coaches Hall of Fame just two short years later. On Wednesday, his influence was on full display as former teammates, players, family and friends poured into the street to mourn.</p><h3><b>How did you get this photo?</b></h3><p>I arrived to the scene later than my reporting colleague, Mike O'Brien, as I was coming from another assignment in Lansing, where a tornado devastated residents earlier this week. By the time I made it to Auburn Gresham, he had already conducted two interviews and walked away to write a quick brief to break the story. So I came in solo and tried to use context clues to figure out who may be Bankston's loved one's while also trying to be as respectful as possible of their grief. I hung to the sides and used my long lens to capture emotional moments like this one. I offered my condolences when appropriate, but ultimately tried to minimize my presence in an attempt to be minimally invasive.</p><h3><b>Technical details:</b></h3><ul class="rte2-style-ul"
